al_ozzy_area.blurb: Ozzy is the second-largest cluster of boulders at Moss Rock Preserve, a city-managed park on the edge of Hoover, south of Birmingham. The sandstone here ranges from friendly problems in the V0 to V2 range up through some very hard lines, so a mixed group can find something to do. Long Shot and General Lee are the easier benchmark problems, and Re-ignition is the one for strong climbers. Expect sloping holds and a few tall, committing problems; bring a good pad and spotters. Weekends can bring a crowd.
al_ozzy_area.parking_note: Use the boulder field lot off Preserve Parkway inside the park; a signed trailhead leads from there into the woods and out to the boulders.

al_ten_pins_area.blurb: Ten Pins is a bouldering sector in the heart of Horse Pens 40, a privately run park on top of Chandler Mountain near Steele. It sits only a few minutes' walk behind the camp store, which makes it an easy first stop. The sandstone is slopey, and the problems lean toward the easy and moderate end, with a handful of hard ones up to V8. Popeye and Mariachi are the best-known lines. Slopers grip best when it is cool and dry, so fall through early spring is the prime window.

al_lizard_wall.blurb: Lizard Wall is a steep sandstone sport wall in Little River Canyon, near Fort Payne. The climbing is technical and powerful: crisp edges, underclings and side pulls lead into a juggy roof that caps much of the wall. Most routes fall in the 5.12 range, with a few 5.11s and 5.13s, so it suits strong, experienced sport climbers. It tends to stay dry when other canyon walls are soaked, which makes it a popular rainy-day choice. Cardboard Cowboy is a good place to start on the harder grades.
al_lizard_wall.parking_note: Drive roughly six miles down the canyon road and use the pull-out on the left side.
al_lizard_wall.approach: A trail leaves the road to the left and drops to a short downclimb, now eased by a ladder and fixed lines. Continue right past a waterfall and hop across the creek rocks to reach the wall.

al_crazy_house_the.blurb: The Crazy House is a sandstone sport crag in Little River Canyon, forming the second half of the Tourist Wall near Fort Payne. Nearly all of the routes sit between 5.11 and 5.12, so it is a place for climbers already comfortable on steep, sustained canyon sport climbing, with just a few easier lines and a handful of harder ones. Bitless and Rocktoberfest are the approachable classics at the lower end of the range. The walk in is short and the trailhead is easy to miss.
al_crazy_house_the.parking_note: About four miles down the canyon road, park in the gravel lot on the left.
al_crazy_house_the.approach: Follow the trail down a series of ramps from the lot. The start of the trail is easy to walk past, so look carefully.

al_toomsuba.blurb: Toomsuba is a south-facing sandstone sport wall in Little River Canyon, near Fort Payne. It takes full sun, which makes it a favorite on cold days, and it handles light rain though not a downpour. The routes are hard and steep: most are 5.12, with a good number of 5.13s and a few 5.11s, so it mainly suits strong sport climbers. Toomsuba, Fight Club and Skin Changer are among the standouts. The descent to the base involves a scramble and a downclimb that needs care, especially when wet.
al_toomsuba.parking_note: Use the pull-offs just before Wolf Creek Overlook, around four and a half miles down the canyon road.
al_toomsuba.approach: A steep scramble and downclimb leads from the road to the base of the wall; take extra care if the rock is wet.

al_griffin_falls.blurb: Griffin Falls is a compact band of sandstone near Collinsville in northeast Alabama, set beside a waterfall that drops onto boulders below. It mixes sport and trad on a modest wall, with most routes between 5.8 and 5.11 and a few harder sport lines. Knife Crack is the classic trad line, while Smashing Pumpkins and Steeplechase are the well-known sport climbs. There are also a few boulder problems. The parking area is small, so sharing rides helps.
al_griffin_falls.parking_note: From Highway 68 near Collinsville, turn onto the gravel road just after the creek bridge at the foot of the hill, then continue to a small second bridge and use the pull-off on the right.

al_scc_property.blurb: The SCC Property is the climber-owned stretch of the Steele cliff line, a long band of sandstone roughly 80 to 100 feet tall in northeast Alabama. The climbing here is mostly traditional, with a few sport lines mixed in, and most routes land between 5.9 and 5.11, so it suits climbers building up on gear. Lone Wolf On the Far Ridge and Suspended Animation are the two best-known lines. The cliff on either side is privately owned, so stay within the boundary signs. Horse Pens 40 is a short drive up the mountain.
al_scc_property.parking_note: Take the shared private drive and keep right at the split; the climbers' lot is at the end, with a composting toilet at one corner.

al_trussville_boulders.blurb: Trussville Boulders is a small cluster of about five boulders in the woods of the Trussville Sports Complex, northeast of Birmingham. The problems are friendly: from the easiest warm-ups through V4, with the bulk in the V0 to V3 range, which makes it a good spot for newer boulderers and families. The area is lightly developed, so a brush helps with dirt and moss. It shares the woods with disc golfers, so keep pads and spotters out of the throwing lanes.
al_trussville_boulders.parking_note: Park in the lot north of the baseball fields, where the disc golf course begins.
al_trussville_boulders.approach: A small trail leaves the northeast corner of that lot and the boulders appear soon after you enter the woods. If it is hard to find, start at the first disc golf hole and follow the paved path beside the river, then climb the hill on your right.

al_the_gorge.blurb: The Gorge is the main bouldering zone at Noccalula Falls Park in Gadsden, in a wooded sandstone gorge where tumbled boulders lie along the creek and up the slopes. Development is still young. The problems cluster in the V3 to V6 range, with a few easier and a couple of harder ones, so it is best for climbers past the beginner stage. Take care with pads on the steep, vegetated ground and stay on the existing paths.
al_the_gorge.parking_note: Use the large lot in front of the chapel and campground on the north side of the park.
al_the_gorge.approach: From the north lot, follow the Black Creek Trail to the Gorge Trail. Descend by the scramble or the wooden stairs, then turn left at the bottom to reach the boulders.

al_cherokee_bluffs.blurb: Cherokee Bluffs is a sport crag on public land near Tallassee, east of Montgomery, and it is the main sport climbing in central Alabama. The cliff line is short, with a mix of sport, some trad, top-rope lines and a few boulder problems. Most routes are 5.8 to 5.11, so there is plenty for intermediate climbers. Slim Jim, Ka-Dunk A-Dunk and A Good Life are the picks. Many lines are fairly new and can use a clean, so a brush is handy. The hike from the lot is short.
al_cherokee_bluffs.parking_note: Drive to the end of Gold Mine Road, down the hill and along the dirt road beside the river, where the lot is.
al_cherokee_bluffs.approach: A short walk from the lot: take the John B. Scott trail, or walk the road around the gate for a few hundred yards until you see wooden steps on the right that climb to the cliff.
